title: Constant approximation
goal: Make the simplest possible estimate of $f(x)$ near a known home-base point $x = a$: just use the known height $f(a)$ itself.

beforeThis.skill: Think of this as "step 0" of Taylor polynomials: if $x$ is super close to $a$ (like $993$ is close to $1000$), $f(x)$ is roughly $f(a)$.

seeIt.title: Taylor series (Ch. 11 of Essence of Calculus)
seeIt.creator: 3Blue1Brown
seeIt.watchFor: Pictures how polynomial approximations start with a constant match $f(a)$ at a nearby base point.

slowWalkthrough.title: Calculus 2 Lecture 9.9: Approximation of Functions by Taylor Polynomials
slowWalkthrough.creator: Professor Leonard

questions.asking: Compare the trade-off between accuracy at $x = 0$ and ease of mental calculation when choosing $g(0)$ versus $h(0)$ to estimate $f(0)$.
questions.statement: The graph below shows three curves. The black curve is $y = f(x)$, the red curve is $y = g(x) = 1 + 2\sin(1 + x)$, and the blue curve is $y = h(x) = 0.7$. If you want to estimate $f(0)$, what might cause you to use $g(0)$? What might cause you to use $h(0)$?

figures.alt: Graph showing an oscillating black curve y = f(x), a red curve y = g(x) that hugs y = f(x) closely near x = 0, and a horizontal blue line y = h(x) = 0.7 that intersects y = f(x) near x = 0.

questions.asking: Choose a nearby input $a$ where $\log(a)$ is known exactly, use that constant value to estimate $\log(0.93)$, and sketch $y = \log x$ alongside the horizontal line.
questions.statement:
Use a constant approximation to estimate the value of $\log(x)$ when $x = 0.93$. Sketch the curve $y = f(x)$ and your constant approximation.

(Remember that we use $\log x$ to mean the natural logarithm of $x$, $\log_e x$.)

questions.asking: Since $10.1$ is right next to $10$, the zeroth-order (constant) approximation just uses the exact value at $a = 10$: $10^3 = 1000$.
questions.statement: Use a constant approximation to estimate the value of $10.1^3$. Your estimation should be something you can calculate in your head.
